        Overnight grain markets were mixed with wheat trading lower, beans higher, and corn caught in between.  Soybeans are supported early on by headline demand after reports that Chinese state buyers purchased 8-10 cargoes of US beans for December and forward delivery.  The USDA reported an 8 am flash sale of 470 tmt (8 cargoes) of beans to China. 
         
        November soybeans are trading 4.5 cents higher.  The near term range bound trade continues.  The calendar spreads are firmer and the Nov-Jan spread traded up to a two-week high.  Domestic bean basis is mostly steady.  The CIF bean bid at the Gulf is soft at +80.  

        The crop progress report showed soybean conditions were unchanged at 47% G\\\/E with P\\\/VP steady at 14%.   92% of the crop is dropping leaves vs the five-year avg of 94%. Bean harvest moved up 21% to 46% complete but remains behind the five-year avg of 50%.  The delays compared to the 5 year averages are most pronounced in IA (-28%), KS (-10%), MI (-11%), NE (-29%), OH (-10%), and SD (-12%).<\\\/span>
         
        In the product trade, meal is a touch firmer while bean oil is lower to start the day.   The Dec-March meal spread is trading lower despite the firmer flat price action.  Bean oil has been under pressure since yesterday’s EPA announcement.  The EPA announced a 100% reallocation of the 2025 SREs.  The EPA is seeking public comment on two proposed approaches to this 1).   EPA would divide the additional 2025 SRE volume equally between the 2026 and 2027 compliance years and 2) EPA would reallocate all the additional 2025 SRW volume to the 2027 compliance year.   EPA will take public comments on the proposal until December 4, 2026.  Despite the price response in bean oil, this was seen as a positive demand outcome by restoring 100% of the biofuel volume impacted by the SREs.  Board crush margins are off by a nickel to $2.58\\\/bushel.  Tomorrow we’ll get the September NOPA crush data where the highlights will likely be the amount of crush lost to limited soybean supply along with the ongoing tightening of bean oil stocks.  
         
        The outside markets feature December heating oil trading into a new contract high before reversing modestly lower, crude oil is $1.20 higher and within’ $2 of contract highs.  The US dollar index is .43 pts higher printing a fresh 18 month high following the CPI data that showed inflation was hotter than expected with traders pricing an almost 50% chance for an October rate hike now.

          Corn Morning Update & Commentary:

          Overnight, the corn market leaned a little easier, finishing either side of one cent lower by the morning pause.  The week so far has been a choppy one as traders re-position and sort out their feelings following a series of USDA report surprises.  The broader ag narrative today is focused on a fresh round of China soy purchases; the export news on corn was less exciting with Taiwan passing on US\\\/Brazil corn.  Making matters worse on this front is a firm US Dollar, which is poking into a new one-and-a-half year high after a warm CPI (consumer inflation) print.  May help keep the southern hemisphere in the corn driver’s seat for a time yet, though we think in the end U.S. corn export potential remains excellent.  EU corn futures have firmed significantly this week, and we suspect they will raise their take of U.S. bushels this year?  Late yesterday, the USDA reported 33% of U.S. corn was harvested, slightly lagging expectations (and the five year average of 39%).  91% of corn is mature, so it is ready; likely a matter of firming-up soils after a very wet conclusion to September?  The next couple of days deliver scattered rains to portions of the Midwest, though we do not expect them to be majorly disruptive.   6-10 & 8-14 day maps are warm and wet on the follow, which should keep farmers motivated.
           
          Corn futures trade was mixed Tuesday; the lows were made on the night session open, and the highs shortly after the day’s opening bell.  Corn finished the day steady to one cent lower, near the middle of a ten cent daily price range.  Funds are estimated net long roughly 245,000 delta-adjusted corn contracts after meaningful liquidation pre\\\/post USDA report.  Cash trade was mixed.  The weekly grain inspections report was near-expected for corn.  For the week ended October 8th, U.S. exporters shipped 1.3 million metric tons (mmt) of corn, down slightly from the prior week’s 1.4 mmt, but slightly ahead of year ago’s 1.2 mmt.  Usual suspects Mexico, Korea, and Japan, were top destinations.   MYTD inspections are still running slightly ahead of last year (8.45 mmt vs. 8.02 mmt) one full month in, though outstanding sales (booked but not shipped) are lagging slightly.  The weekly EIA report has been delayed to Thursday morning due to Monday’s federal holiday.  Biofuel industry received some good news in that recent small refiner exempted gallons would be fully re-allocated to larger players in future years.   Likely won’t drive much of a price reaction, though, as ethanol blending margins are already at absurdly attractive levels??

          October 14, 2026 <\\\/strong> <\\\/p>

          MARKETS <\\\/h2>

          <\\\/h2>

          The cash market is disappearing before our eyes. Show lists were larger in Texas and Kansas but smaller in Nebraska. Ideas are developing that northern feedlots are more current than the past few weeks. Some cattle in both Kansas and Texas sold with a negotiated base price of $227 but were not reported in the cash trade. USDA has failed to release any plan to correct non-reporting. The pool of cash transactions continues to dwindle. <\\\/p>

          One unique feature of beef demand has been resilience. High prices normally with most products cause buyers to switch to other alternatives, buy cheaper versions of the same product, eat less of the product or stop eating it. Beef demand in large part has survived the price increases of the last two years. That doesnt mean demand cant be damaged in the future by price, but it is a reflection of the importance most consumers place on the desirability of the product. Economists would call the demand curve for beef largely inelastic. <\\\/p>

          Late trading in the north moved live prices from earlier $218 to $220-$223. Dressed prices were mainly $345 with some up to $350. Some light trade in Texas and Kansas was reported at $226. <\\\/p>

          This week slaughter volumes was 535,000 head - 13,000 under the previous week and in line with current retail demand for beef. It fell 17,000 under last year. Plant attendance is normal and changes in weekly slaughter will be driven by supply and demand. Processors have maintained profitability since July - the longest period during the past few years. The status for fed supplies will remain tight through year end especially in the south. <\\\/p>

          Benchmarking <\\\/a> . On Tuesday of each week, USDA releases a weighted average price report for all cattle sold the previous week. The report summarizes the distributed price levels for each category of sale such as Negotiated\\\/Formula\\\/Forward Contracts. Beef producers are able to measure the marketing price for their cattle compared to the national averages. <\\\/p>

          The Comprehensive Fed Cattle Weekly Report <\\\/a> offers the most current information on the current status of fed cattle being harvested. The report is published each Tuesday and includes the previous weeks change in carcass weights and quality grading. The latest report shows carcass weights at 953#, up 1# from the prior week, and 14# heavier than last year. The combined steer and heifer weights can easily be influenced when the proportion of steers to heifers in the weekly slaughter changes. Quality grade was up .1% from the previous week at 87.3. The quality grade remains near historic highs as cattle are fed to heavier weights. <\\\/p>

          The Weekly Steer and Heifer Grading Report <\\\/a> <\\\/a> reflects regional supplies of choice and prime cattle and often is determinative of regional differences in live prices. The report also indicates the current status of fed cattle offerings in each area. <\\\/p>

          Forward Cattle Contracts <\\\/a> : Forward contracts are always a portion of the inventories the processors maintain for slaughter. Offered basis levels will move up and down as processors want to add to forward contracts or not. The driver in forward purchases of cattle will always be forward sales of beef. Packers will always be willing to take a price risk off the producers plate in return for an extra margin. The movement of futures prices, either up or down, will relate to the number of forward contracts. <\\\/p>

          Formula and Negotiated Grids. The Price and Distribution Report <\\\/a> delineates the various selling methods and net results. <\\\/p>

          The Cattle Contracts Report <\\\/a> details the percent of contracts by volume of cattle and by number of contracts for selling cattle. Formula selling that was once the largest marketing method and still is, but is losing ground to negotiated grids where the premiums and discounts are set but the base price is negotiated. <\\\/p>

          Beef Feature Activity Index. <\\\/a> <\\\/p>

          USDA Prime cuts are carving out a larger slice of the grocery offerings. This is changing consumer decisions at the meat counter. Spreads between choice offerings and prime cuts historically have been wide and with more product and difficulty moving expensive cuts, many Prime cuts now sell at smaller incremental price spreads to choice causing many consumers to upgrade their purchases. Casualities in this change have been branded or all natural products that are commonly passed over by consumers. <\\\/p>

          The Cutout <\\\/a> . Box prices were flat. The lean beef prices have struggled to hold ground under pressure from the imported beef. This past weeks slaughter volume jumped from the previous weeks small number to the largest volume since January. Slaughter volumes will continue to be dictated by processing margins and government intervention. <\\\/p>

          It is important to remember that spot box prices are much like spot cash prices for live cattle. Most boxes are sold under formulas and do not always have the same fluctuations as the spot market. <\\\/p>

          Replacement markets <\\\/strong> <\\\/p>

          October and November are the largest marketing periods of the year for replacement cattle. Demand for replacements is high and recent rains provided broad coverage of the nation leading to new grazing opportunities for cattle for growing and breeding. The problem simply stated is a shortage of animals to fill those fields of grazing opportunities. Those buyers closely examining the future outcome of todays purchases, based on deferred cattle futures, will not find financial rewards at the end of the line. Much of the nations farm tracts will be left empty of cattle reserving the crop to be harvested for grain. <\\\/p>

          Weather will always influence the market for replacement cattle. The main grain belt in the southern plains, where many cattle are grazed on winter wheat, has enjoyed generous rains. Most fields have been planted and some have an emerged crop. Warm weather will now be important to plant growth and grazing opportunities. The wildcard for a year that could provide the largest winter grazing in decades is availability of cattle. There simply may not be enough cattle to stock winter grazing sites. Recent rains in the desert southwest has activated hopes for desert grazing and the opening of the border will provide some limited supply of cattle. <\\\/p>

          Movement from Mexico has featured groups of heavy cattle nearing finish in Mexican feedlots. These cattle will move to U.S. feedyards for a short finishing period before being sold to processors. Very few light Mexican cattle are being offered because of generous rains across Chihuahua and Sonora. <\\\/p>

          Seasonally health problems, that can occur anytime with the stress of weaning, worsen for unweaned calves during the fall. Many operators have suffered the penalty paid when they buy fresh weaned calves and experience usually large death loss. Not only can death loss percentages jump, but also sick calves present a constant labor requirement and long term performance impairment. A $50 cwt. spread between weaned and unweaned calves is large, but sometimes justified. The spreads between weaned and unweaned calves is widening. Knowing more about the background of new purchases can be helpful including full health records. <\\\/p>

          October 14, 2026<\\\/span>

          Monthly wind generation in ISO-NE is about 68% higher than last year<\\\/span><\\\/a><\\\/span><\\\/h1>

          <\\\/span><\\\/p>

          Data source: <\\\/strong>U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-930, Hourly Electric Grid Monitor<\\\/a>
          <\\\/span><\\\/div>

          Monthly wind generation in the first nine months of 2026 was an average of 68% higher compared with the same period in 2025 in ISO New England<\\\/a> (ISO-NE):<\\\/span><\\\/p>


          <\\\/span><\\\/p>

          • Monthly generation from wind was highest in September of this year at 668.9 gigawatthours (GWh), more than double generation levels from September 2025 and nearly 10% higher than this year’s previous high in March.<\\\/li>
          • Increased wind generation is the result of growing capacity additions<\\\/a> in the ISO-NE region. Regional wind capacity increased 47% so far in 2026 to 2.5 gigawatts, following a 12% increase in capacity in 2025.<\\\/li>
          • Daily wind generation peaked on October 6, 2026, at about 47.3 GWh, 1% higher than the previous peak that occurred on September 10, 2026.<\\\/li>
          • Total wind generation for the first nine months of 2026 was 4,619 GWh, 1.9% more than last year’s annual total of 4,533 GWh.<\\\/li><\\\/ul><\\\/div>\"","timestamp":"2026-10-14 12:42:11","filename":"","hot":"","type":""},{"nid":"1441658448","categories":"3","source":"QT","headline":"Fed Beige Book: twelve Federal Reserve Districts reported moderate growth in economic activity.","body":"\"

Corn: Slightly lower day as dollar firms to multi-month high","body":"\"
            Afternoon Corn:  
             
            Corn futures maintained the week’s quietly choppy tenor, spending most of the day slightly lower.  The market would close out the day 1-2 cents lower, which was the mid-point of a six cent daily price range.  Managed Money likely slipped out of a little more length today; we think they are going home net long roughly 240,000 delta-adjusted corn contracts.  Cash trade was mixed, governed largely by the composition of local harvest.
             
            Exports were a theme today.   Soybeans captured early headlines via a sizable Chinese purchase; that market responded with a ‘buy the rumor, sell the fact,’ move?  Export news in corn has been less favorable of late, though that is not unusual for the season.  Taiwan passed on their tender for US or Brazil origin corn, and recent South Korean business is believed to have traded mostly out of South America.  Making matters worse of late is a firm US Dollar, which is poking into a new one-and-a-half year high today after a warm CPI (consumer inflation) print.  Firmness in the US Dollar may help keep the southern hemisphere in the corn driver’s seat for the moment, though we think in the end U.S. corn export potential remains excellent.  To cite one example, EU corn futures have firmed significantly this week, and we suspect they will raise their take of U.S. bushels this year?  Note the weekly export sales report has been pushed to Friday due to Monday’s federal holiday.
             
            Also with an eye toward the holiday, the weekly EIA energy report is due out tomorrow late morning.  We expect ethanol production will continue to recover following seasonal maintenance; we are expecting it to rise another +1% to +2% this week.  Blender demand should bounce back, while exports might relax a little.  Disappearance should be enough though to keep drawing stocks; we look for it to decline another -1% wk\\\/wk.  Ethanol futures have given back all of Monday’s gains over the past two sessions; we think an average Midwest plant is earning 45-50 c\\\/gal net profits, close to the mid-point of a seven month range.
             
            Elsewhere, other end-user markets remained split between livestock (weak) and milk (firm).  Milk futures have ripped over +10% over the past six trading sessions?  Weekly USDA reporting found broiler egg sets up +3% yr\\\/yr with chick placements +1% higher.   Outside markets leaned very risk-off today; metals and stocks were under pressure, while the US Dollar and oil were firm.  The next couple of days deliver scattered rains to the Midwest, particularly the south and east, though we do not expect them to be majorly disruptive to harvest.   6-10 & 8-14 day maps are warm and wet on the follow, which should keep farmers motivated to get back after it?   Late yesterday, the USDA reported 33% of U.S. corn was harvested, slightly lagging expectations (and the five year average of 39%).
             
            In the options, volatility eroded a little further.  Mid-morning, over 1,000 March $6.50 Calls traded at one cent.  Calendar spreads were slightly firmer up-front, but softer between marketing years.   Corn gained a little ground on the beans but lost a little to wheat.  On the charts, post-report trade builds another layer of overhead resistance into the charts with selling on rallies back to $5 CZ highly likely.  Report day lows of $4.70 CZ will stand as initial support moving forward; this area was also a full two-thirds Fibonacci retracement of the July-Aug rally.  Futures are mildly oversold but not egregiously-so with an RSI in the mid 20’s.   The August gap higher was filled on the weekly chart, which may also contribute to reduced upside market enthusiasm for now.   Note, the weekly chart also features notable support around $4.65 basis any front-month contract.

","body":"\"
            The soybean market traded firmer overnight but was unable to carry that momentum into the day session despite the return of Chinese bean purchases during the biscuit break.  The buy the rumor sell the fact price action reflected the pressure from expanding harvest and strength in the dollar which is a negative influence for export sensitive commodities.  
             
            November soybeans settled 6.5 cents lower and 16 cents off the overnight high.  The chart is testing support at the lower end of its recent trading range.  The calendar spreads were firm up front as pressure from the index fund roll has abated.  The Nov-Jan spread gaining 1.5 to a 2-week high at a 14.75 carry.   In the inter-market spread action, beans lost to corn for the third session in a row following Friday’s dramatic crop report move the other direction.  Domestic bean basis was mostly steady to lower with the gut slot of harvest upon us for the next few weeks despite some short term, regional disruptions expected by rains.  The CIF bean bid at the Gulf was up 2 to +82.  
             
            Ahead of tomorrow’s NOPA crush report, the average trade estimate on September crush is 203.7 mb, down from 205.4 mb in August but up from the September of 2025 crush of 197.8 mb.  If achieved this would represent a new record for the month despite soybean supply tightness that forced some plants to reduce their crush.  Oil stocks at the end of September were estimated on average at 1.116 bln lbs down from 1.201 bln lbs in August and 1.243 bln lbs in September of 2025.  If realized, this would be the tightest monthly oil stocks since November of 2024. 
             
            Tomorrow, we’ll also get a monthly Conab update on Brazilian production potential in the morning.   It is too early in the growing\\\/planting season down there to make any meaningful adjustments to crop expectations.  Planting is off to a positive start is about all you can say. 
             
            In the product trade, bean oil has been under pressure since yesterday’s midday EPA announcement including a .96 drop today.  The EPA announced a 100% reallocation of the 2025 SREs with the only question being whether those volumes are divided between 2026 and 2027 or they all fall into the 2027 compliance year.  Despite the negative price response in bean oil, this is seen as a positive demand outcome by restoring 100% of the biofuel volume impacted by the SREs.  The oil share spread retreated to a 2.5 week low to 47.91%.  Meal was the beneficiary of the oil share spreading which supported a $1.3 flat price gain and a bounce back in the bull spreads.  Board crush margins were a penny easier to $2.62\\\/bushel. 
             
            Elsewhere in the news, the USDA reported an 8 am flash sale of 470 tmt of beans to China. <\\\/span>

            The crop progress report showed soybean conditions were unchanged at 47% G\\\/E with P\\\/VP steady at 14%.   92% of the crop is dropping leaves vs the five-year avg of 94%. Bean harvest moved up 21% to 46% complete but remains behind the five-year avg of 50%.  The delays compared to the 5 year averages are most pronounced in IA (-28%), KS (-10%), MI (-11%), NE (-29%), OH (-10%), and SD (-12%).
             
            Brazil soybean exports in October are projected to reach 6.55 mmt vs. 6.18 mmt estimated the previous week, according to Anec.  Meal exports 2.55 mmt vs. 2.09 mmt.  Corn exports 6.41 mmt vs. 5.34 mmt.
             
            “ASA applauds Administrator Zeldin and the Trump Administration for keeping their commitment to farmers and proposing to restore 100% of biofuel volume impacted by 2025 small refinery exemption actions,” said ASA Vice President Dave Walton, an Iowa soybean farmer. “Soybean farmers are navigating a tough farm economy, and the administration’s strong domestic biofuel policies will continue to drive much-needed market demand in the U.S. We are encouraged by today’s proposal and urge EPA to get it across the finish line quickly.”  ASA urges EPA to finalize this supplemental rulemaking to reallocate biofuel volumes as quickly as possible.

            Futures:<\\\/span><\\\/u><\\\/em><\\\/strong><\\\/p>

            Outside market influence seemed prevalent during the early part of the day as the US Dollar rallied into a fresh 18-month high following the CPI data that showed inflation was hotter than expected with traders now pricing an almost 50% chance for an Oct rate hike. But the wheat markets battled back over the latter half of the day and finished well off their lows and right up near their highs for the day.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            Dec Chicago wheat traded four lower early in the night and slipped to six lower during the early morning before rallying to within a penny of even late, only to weaken into the pause and finish four lower. Price action through the early part of the day stayed between unchanged and six lower. A mid-morning eight-cent pop sparked a rally that continued into the final hour, with the market making their session’s highs near the close before finishing four higher. <\\\/span>Dec KC wheat traded four lower early in the night and slipped to seven lower during the early morning before rallying a nickel, only to weaken again into the pause and finish five lower. After a mostly three to seven lower start to the day, futures fell to nine lower, and in doing so, moved into a three-month low. But then the market found a bid late morning and futures rallied more than ten cents, extending gains to four cents into the close before finishing three higher. <\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            Headline news:<\\\/span><\\\/u><\\\/em><\\\/strong><\\\/p>

            USDA weekly export sales will be out Friday morning, delayed one day because of Monday’s gov’t Holiday.  <\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            France Agrimer raised their forecast for French soft wheat exports outside the EU by 200 TMT up to 6.5 MMT and lowered their forecast for exports inside the EU by 100 TMT down to 7.0 MMT. They also lowered their 2026\\\/27 soft wheat ending stocks forecast by 300 TMT down to 2.7 MMT.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            Ukraine’s winter wheat planting is said to be more than 67% complete as of Tuesday, with more than 3 mil hectares planted.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/span><\\\/u><\\\/em><\\\/strong><\\\/p>

            Export business around this week:<\\\/span><\\\/u><\\\/em><\\\/strong> <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            ** Algeria’s OAIC is now thought to have bought upwards of 720 TMT of opt origin milling wheat in their tender that closed on Tuesday. Sources include Baltic Sea region wheat, including Russian supplies shipped from Baltic ports, plus Romanian, Bulgarian and Argentine wheat. Purchases were thought to be between $326 and $326.50\\\/mt C&F. In their last reported milling wheat import tender in mid-Sept, the OAIC bought ~ 500 TMT, paying between $319 and $321\\\/mt C&F. Meaning they paid a higher price in this tender than they paid a month ago, despite futures falling around 70 cents.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            ** Jordan passed on all offers and did not make a purchase in their 120 TMT opt origin milling wheat tender.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            Corn Morning Update<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            QT News - Top News<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            *Weekly USDA Export sales delayed until Friday due to Monday's holiday<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            -- Jordan's state grain buyer on Thursday set October 21st as the offer deadline for a tender seeking up to 120,000 mt of feed Barley.  The grain is expected for shipment between January 1 through February 28.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            -- State run fishery of South Korea on Thursday announced a tender seeking around 56,000 mt of Rice, offers are due October 29th.  The total sought includes 15,000 mt of US origin rice, 6,600 mt from Vietnam, and the remainder can be sourced from any other origin.  The grain is for delivery between Jan 1 2027 through Sept 30, 2027<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            -- Expana analysts Thursday lowered their EU 26\\\/27 corn production forecast by -1.3 mln mt to 44.9 mln mt, the previous forecast at 46.2 mln mt was said to be the lowest output since 1992, the newest forecast would be a new low near 1990 production levels.  The reduction will likely result in the EU being more reliant on imports from outside Ukraine's traditional supplies.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            -- Expana analysts Thursday slightly raised their EU 26\\\/27 corn production forecast by +0.1 mln mt to 51.7 mln mt; 26\\\/27 EU soft wheat production was left unchanged at 126.1 mln mt<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            -- Ukraine's ag minister Thursday estimated October 1-13 agriculture goods exports at 1.125 mln mt, roughly half the country's export potential  The total included 670,000 mt of grain, 184,000 mt of oilseeds and 138,000 mt of vegoil.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            -- Russia's IFX media outlet Wednesday reported the country's grain harvest so far has totaled more than 126 million metric tons<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            -- InterContinental Exchange (ICE) on Wednesday announced plans to start trading live cattle futures, feeder cattle futures, and lean hog futures on December 7th.  The first contracts listed will be for June 2027 for physically delivered live cattle futures.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            Business activity rose sharply in New York State in October, according to firms responding to the <\\\/span>Empire State Manufacturing Survey<\\\/em>. The headline general business conditions index climbed eighteen points to 25.5, its highest level in nearly five years. 

            New orders increased markedly and shipments grew. Unfilled orders rose, delivery times lengthened substantially, and supply availability worsened further. Inventories increased. Employment continued to rise modestly and the average workweek rose. The pace of input and selling price increases remained elevated. October 14, 2026 <\\\/strong> <\\\/p>

MARKETS <\\\/h2>

<\\\/h2>

The cash market is disappearing before our eyes. Show lists were larger in Texas and Kansas but smaller in Nebraska.         Overnight grain markets were mixed with wheat trading lower, beans higher, and corn caught in between.  Soybeans are supported early on by headline demand after reports that Chinese state buyers purchased 8-10 cargoes of US beans for December and forward delivery.  The USDA reported an 8 am flash sale of 470 tmt (8 cargoes) of beans to China. 
         
        November soybeans are trading 4.5 cents higher.  The near term range bound trade continues.  The calendar spreads are firmer and the Nov-Jan spread traded up to a two-week high.  Domestic bean basis is mostly steady.  The CIF bean bid at the Gulf is soft at +80.  

        The crop progress report showed soybean conditions were unchanged at 47% G\\\/E with P\\\/VP steady at 14%.   92% of the crop is dropping leaves vs the five-year avg of 94%. Bean harvest moved up 21% to 46% complete but remains behind the five-year avg of 50%.  The delays compared to the 5 year averages are most pronounced in IA (-28%), KS (-10%), MI (-11%), NE (-29%), OH (-10%), and SD (-12%).<\\\/span>
         
        In the product trade, meal is a touch firmer while bean oil is lower to start the day.   The Dec-March meal spread is trading lower despite the firmer flat price action.  Bean oil has been under pressure since yesterday’s EPA announcement.  The EPA announced a 100% reallocation of the 2025 SREs.  The EPA is seeking public comment on two proposed approaches to this 1).   EPA would divide the additional 2025 SRE volume equally between the 2026 and 2027 compliance years and 2) EPA would reallocate all the additional 2025 SRW volume to the 2027 compliance year.   EPA will take public comments on the proposal until December 4, 2026.  Despite the price response in bean oil, this was seen as a positive demand outcome by restoring 100% of the biofuel volume impacted by the SREs.  Board crush margins are off by a nickel to $2.58\\\/bushel.  Tomorrow we’ll get the September NOPA crush data where the highlights will likely be the amount of crush lost to limited soybean supply along with the ongoing tightening of bean oil stocks.  
         
        The outside markets feature December heating oil trading into a new contract high before reversing modestly lower, crude oil is $1.20 higher and within’ $2 of contract highs.  The US dollar index is .43 pts higher printing a fresh 18 month high following the CPI data that showed inflation was hotter than expected with traders pricing an almost 50% chance for an October rate hike now. 
         
         
        In the news:
        • Grain traders cited by Reuters on Wednesday say between 8 to 10 Panamax size cargoes of US Soybeans were bought this week by Chinese state buyers.  The soy is for shipment from December and beyond.  Prices were said to be $3.10 to $3.20 over January CBOT corn futures.  These purchases are the first since the Trump-Xi summit back in September.<\\\/li>
        • Brazil soybean exports in October are projected to reach 6.55 mmt vs. 6.18 mmt estimated the previous week, according to Anec.   Meal exports 2.55 mmt vs. 2.09 mmt.  Corn exports 6.41 mmt vs. 5.34 mmt.<\\\/li>
        • Chinese customs data released Wednesday placed the country's September Soybean imports at 11.88 mln mt, off -7.7% from the year ago month, and were off -2.1% from August's 12.14 mln mt of soy imports.  Over the first nine months of 2026 soy imports totaled 86.08 mln mt.<\\\/li>
        • Sinograin announced they will auction 504,000 mt of state held imported Soybeans on October 20th.<\\\/li>
        • Top executive with China's COFCO Oils & Oilseeds said the country's crushing industry is experiencing severe overcapacity.  They estimate by the end of this year daily soybean crush capacity will top 520,000 mt.<\\\/li>
        • Top executive with China's COFCO Oils & Oilseeds said animal per capita protein consumption is gradually peaking, and China's soymeal consumption may have plateaued with wider acceptance of low-protein feed technologies.<\\\/li>
        • “ASA applauds Administrator Zeldin and the Trump Administration for keeping their commitment to farmers and proposing to restore 100% of biofuel volume impacted by 2025 small refinery exemption actions,” said ASA Vice President Dave Walton, an Iowa soybean farmer. “Soybean farmers are navigating a tough farm economy, and the administration’s strong domestic biofuel policies will continue to drive much-needed market demand in the U.S. We are encouraged by today’s proposal and urge EPA to get it across the finish line quickly.”  ASA urges EPA to finalize this supplemental rulemaking to reallocate biofuel volumes as quickly as possible.<\\\/li>

        • Euronext Paris February rapeseed futures on Wednesday are trading -1.75 euros lower at 557.5 euros\\\/mt<\\\/li>

          Corn Morning Update & Commentary:

          Overnight, the corn market leaned a little easier, finishing either side of one cent lower by the morning pause.  The week so far has been a choppy one as traders re-position and sort out their feelings following a series of USDA report surprises.  The broader ag narrative today is focused on a fresh round of China soy purchases; the export news on corn was less exciting with Taiwan passing on US\\\/Brazil corn.  Making matters worse on this front is a firm US Dollar, which is poking into a new one-and-a-half year high after a warm CPI (consumer inflation) print.  May help keep the southern hemisphere in the corn driver’s seat for a time yet, though we think in the end U.S. corn export potential remains excellent.  EU corn futures have firmed significantly this week, and we suspect they will raise their take of U.S. bushels this year?  Late yesterday, the USDA reported 33% of U.S. corn was harvested, slightly lagging expectations (and the five year average of 39%).  91% of corn is mature, so it is ready; likely a matter of firming-up soils after a very wet conclusion to September?  The next couple of days deliver scattered rains to portions of the Midwest, though we do not expect them to be majorly disruptive.   6-10 & 8-14 day maps are warm and wet on the follow, which should keep farmers motivated.
           
          Corn futures trade was mixed Tuesday; the lows were made on the night session open, and the highs shortly after the day’s opening bell.  Corn finished the day steady to one cent lower, near the middle of a ten cent daily price range.  Funds are estimated net long roughly 245,000 delta-adjusted corn contracts after meaningful liquidation pre\\\/post USDA report.  Cash trade was mixed.  The weekly grain inspections report was near-expected for corn.  For the week ended October 8th, U.S. exporters shipped 1.3 million metric tons (mmt) of corn, down slightly from the prior week’s 1.4 mmt, but slightly ahead of year ago’s 1.2 mmt.  Usual suspects Mexico, Korea, and Japan, were top destinations.   MYTD inspections are still running slightly ahead of last year (8.45 mmt vs. 8.02 mmt) one full month in, though outstanding sales (booked but not shipped) are lagging slightly.  The weekly EIA report has been delayed to Thursday morning due to Monday’s federal holiday.  Biofuel industry received some good news in that recent small refiner exempted gallons would be fully re-allocated to larger players in future years.   Likely won’t drive much of a price reaction, though, as ethanol blending margins are already at absurdly attractive levels??

          -- Traders say Taiwan's MFIG passed on all offers in their 65,000 mt feed Corn tender, prices were said to too high.  The lowest offer was $2.240\\\/mt cf over March CBOT Corn futures.  Only US and Brazil corn was offered, no South African or Argentine corn was offered.
           
          -- Grain traders Wednesday now report 60,000 mt of feed Barley was purchased by Jordan's state grain buyer.  They reportedly paid $307.0\\\/mt cf for LH January shipment.  Another barley tender is expected to be announced soon, with a likely offer deadline on October 21st.
           
          -- France AgriMer Wednesday forecast French 26\\\/27 ending Corn stocks are at 1.1 mln mt, down -400,000 mt from the prior estimate.
           
          -- France AgriMer Wednesday forecast French 26\\\/27 ending Barley stocks are at 1.5 mln mt, down -100,000 mt from the prior estimate.
           
          -- As of October 11, accumulated 26\\\/27 MY EU Corn imports totaled 5.9 mln mt (last report 5.44 mln mt), that compares to the year earlier week's 4.6 mln mt
           
          -- As of October 11, accumulated 26\\\/27 MY EU Barley exports totaled 2.1 mln mt (last report 1.92 mln mt), that compares to the year earlier week's 3.6 mln mt
           
          -- Chinese customs data released Wednesday placed the country's September total meat imports at 418,000 mt, down -6.5% from August meat imports at 447,000 mt.  Over the January-September 2026 period meat imports were 4.44 mln mt, that was off -7.2% from the year earlier period.

          October 14, 2026 <\\\/strong> <\\\/p>

          MARKETS <\\\/h2>

          <\\\/h2>

          The cash market is disappearing before our eyes. Show lists were larger in Texas and Kansas but smaller in Nebraska. Ideas are developing that northern feedlots are more current than the past few weeks. Some cattle in both Kansas and Texas sold with a negotiated base price of $227 but were not reported in the cash trade. USDA has failed to release any plan to correct non-reporting. The pool of cash transactions continues to dwindle. <\\\/p>

          One unique feature of beef demand has been resilience. High prices normally with most products cause buyers to switch to other alternatives, buy cheaper versions of the same product, eat less of the product or stop eating it. Beef demand in large part has survived the price increases of the last two years. That doesnt mean demand cant be damaged in the future by price, but it is a reflection of the importance most consumers place on the desirability of the product. Economists would call the demand curve for beef largely inelastic. <\\\/p>

          Late trading in the north moved live prices from earlier $218 to $220-$223. Dressed prices were mainly $345 with some up to $350. Some light trade in Texas and Kansas was reported at $226. <\\\/p>

          This week slaughter volumes was 535,000 head - 13,000 under the previous week and in line with current retail demand for beef. It fell 17,000 under last year. Plant attendance is normal and changes in weekly slaughter will be driven by supply and demand. Processors have maintained profitability since July - the longest period during the past few years. The status for fed supplies will remain tight through year end especially in the south. <\\\/p>

          Benchmarking <\\\/a> . On Tuesday of each week, USDA releases a weighted average price report for all cattle sold the previous week. The report summarizes the distributed price levels for each category of sale such as Negotiated\\\/Formula\\\/Forward Contracts. Beef producers are able to measure the marketing price for their cattle compared to the national averages. <\\\/p>

          The Comprehensive Fed Cattle Weekly Report <\\\/a> offers the most current information on the current status of fed cattle being harvested. The report is published each Tuesday and includes the previous weeks change in carcass weights and quality grading. The latest report shows carcass weights at 953#, up 1# from the prior week, and 14# heavier than last year. The combined steer and heifer weights can easily be influenced when the proportion of steers to heifers in the weekly slaughter changes. Quality grade was up .1% from the previous week at 87.3. The quality grade remains near historic highs as cattle are fed to heavier weights. <\\\/p>

          The Weekly Steer and Heifer Grading Report <\\\/a> <\\\/a> reflects regional supplies of choice and prime cattle and often is determinative of regional differences in live prices. The report also indicates the current status of fed cattle offerings in each area. <\\\/p>

          Forward Cattle Contracts <\\\/a> : Forward contracts are always a portion of the inventories the processors maintain for slaughter. Offered basis levels will move up and down as processors want to add to forward contracts or not. The driver in forward purchases of cattle will always be forward sales of beef. Packers will always be willing to take a price risk off the producers plate in return for an extra margin. The movement of futures prices, either up or down, will relate to the number of forward contracts. <\\\/p>

          Formula and Negotiated Grids. The Price and Distribution Report <\\\/a> delineates the various selling methods and net results. <\\\/p>

          The Cattle Contracts Report <\\\/a> details the percent of contracts by volume of cattle and by number of contracts for selling cattle. Formula selling that was once the largest marketing method and still is, but is losing ground to negotiated grids where the premiums and discounts are set but the base price is negotiated. <\\\/p>

          Beef Feature Activity Index. <\\\/a> <\\\/p>

          USDA Prime cuts are carving out a larger slice of the grocery offerings. This is changing consumer decisions at the meat counter. Spreads between choice offerings and prime cuts historically have been wide and with more product and difficulty moving expensive cuts, many Prime cuts now sell at smaller incremental price spreads to choice causing many consumers to upgrade their purchases. Casualities in this change have been branded or all natural products that are commonly passed over by consumers. <\\\/p>

          The Cutout <\\\/a> . Box prices were flat. The lean beef prices have struggled to hold ground under pressure from the imported beef. This past weeks slaughter volume jumped from the previous weeks small number to the largest volume since January. Slaughter volumes will continue to be dictated by processing margins and government intervention. <\\\/p>

          It is important to remember that spot box prices are much like spot cash prices for live cattle. Most boxes are sold under formulas and do not always have the same fluctuations as the spot market. <\\\/p>

          Replacement markets <\\\/strong> <\\\/p>

          October and November are the largest marketing periods of the year for replacement cattle. Demand for replacements is high and recent rains provided broad coverage of the nation leading to new grazing opportunities for cattle for growing and breeding. The problem simply stated is a shortage of animals to fill those fields of grazing opportunities. Those buyers closely examining the future outcome of todays purchases, based on deferred cattle futures, will not find financial rewards at the end of the line. Much of the nations farm tracts will be left empty of cattle reserving the crop to be harvested for grain. <\\\/p>

          Weather will always influence the market for replacement cattle. The main grain belt in the southern plains, where many cattle are grazed on winter wheat, has enjoyed generous rains. Most fields have been planted and some have an emerged crop. Warm weather will now be important to plant growth and grazing opportunities. The wildcard for a year that could provide the largest winter grazing in decades is availability of cattle. There simply may not be enough cattle to stock winter grazing sites. Recent rains in the desert southwest has activated hopes for desert grazing and the opening of the border will provide some limited supply of cattle. <\\\/p>

          Movement from Mexico has featured groups of heavy cattle nearing finish in Mexican feedlots. These cattle will move to U.S. feedyards for a short finishing period before being sold to processors. Very few light Mexican cattle are being offered because of generous rains across Chihuahua and Sonora. <\\\/p>

          Seasonally health problems, that can occur anytime with the stress of weaning, worsen for unweaned calves during the fall. Many operators have suffered the penalty paid when they buy fresh weaned calves and experience usually large death loss. Not only can death loss percentages jump, but also sick calves present a constant labor requirement and long term performance impairment. A $50 cwt. spread between weaned and unweaned calves is large, but sometimes justified. The spreads between weaned and unweaned calves is widening. Knowing more about the background of new purchases can be helpful including full health records. <\\\/p>

          <\\\/span><\\\/p>

          Data source: <\\\/strong>U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-930, Hourly Electric Grid Monitor<\\\/a>
          <\\\/span><\\\/div>

          Monthly wind generation in the first nine months of 2026 was an average of 68% higher compared with the same period in 2025 in ISO New England<\\\/a> (ISO-NE):<\\\/span><\\\/p>


          <\\\/span><\\\/p>

          • Monthly generation from wind was highest in September of this year at 668.9 gigawatthours (GWh), more than double generation levels from September 2025 and nearly 10% higher than this year’s previous high in March.<\\\/li>
          • Increased wind generation is the result of growing capacity additions<\\\/a> in the ISO-NE region. Regional wind capacity increased 47% so far in 2026 to 2.5 gigawatts, following a 12% increase in capacity in 2025.<\\\/li>
          • Daily wind generation peaked on October 6, 2026, at about 47.3 GWh, 1% higher than the previous peak that occurred on September 10, 2026.<\\\/li>
          • Total wind generation for the first nine months of 2026 was 4,619 GWh, 1.9% more than last year’s annual total of 4,533 GWh.<\\\/li><\\\/ul><\\\/div>\"","timestamp":"2026-10-14 12:42:11","filename":"","hot":"","type":""},{"nid":"1441658448","categories":"3","source":"QT","headline":"Fed Beige Book: twelve Federal Reserve Districts reported moderate growth in economic activity.","body":"\"

            Afternoon Corn:  
             
            Corn futures maintained the week’s quietly choppy tenor, spending most of the day slightly lower.  The market would close out the day 1-2 cents lower, which was the mid-point of a six cent daily price range.  Managed Money likely slipped out of a little more length today; we think they are going home net long roughly 240,000 delta-adjusted corn contracts.  Cash trade was mixed, governed largely by the composition of local harvest.
             
            Exports were a theme today.   Soybeans captured early headlines via a sizable Chinese purchase; that market responded with a ‘buy the rumor, sell the fact,’ move?  Export news in corn has been less favorable of late, though that is not unusual for the season.  Taiwan passed on their tender for US or Brazil origin corn, and recent South Korean business is believed to have traded mostly out of South America.  Making matters worse of late is a firm US Dollar, which is poking into a new one-and-a-half year high today after a warm CPI (consumer inflation) print.  Firmness in the US Dollar may help keep the southern hemisphere in the corn driver’s seat for the moment, though we think in the end U.S. corn export potential remains excellent.  To cite one example, EU corn futures have firmed significantly this week, and we suspect they will raise their take of U.S. bushels this year?  Note the weekly export sales report has been pushed to Friday due to Monday’s federal holiday.
             
            Also with an eye toward the holiday, the weekly EIA energy report is due out tomorrow late morning.  We expect ethanol production will continue to recover following seasonal maintenance; we are expecting it to rise another +1% to +2% this week.  Blender demand should bounce back, while exports might relax a little.  Disappearance should be enough though to keep drawing stocks; we look for it to decline another -1% wk\\\/wk.  Ethanol futures have given back all of Monday’s gains over the past two sessions; we think an average Midwest plant is earning 45-50 c\\\/gal net profits, close to the mid-point of a seven month range.
             
            Elsewhere, other end-user markets remained split between livestock (weak) and milk (firm).  Milk futures have ripped over +10% over the past six trading sessions?  Weekly USDA reporting found broiler egg sets up +3% yr\\\/yr with chick placements +1% higher.   Outside markets leaned very risk-off today; metals and stocks were under pressure, while the US Dollar and oil were firm.  The next couple of days deliver scattered rains to the Midwest, particularly the south and east, though we do not expect them to be majorly disruptive to harvest.   6-10 & 8-14 day maps are warm and wet on the follow, which should keep farmers motivated to get back after it?   Late yesterday, the USDA reported 33% of U.S. corn was harvested, slightly lagging expectations (and the five year average of 39%).
             
            In the options, volatility eroded a little further.  Mid-morning, over 1,000 March $6.50 Calls traded at one cent.  Calendar spreads were slightly firmer up-front, but softer between marketing years.   Corn gained a little ground on the beans but lost a little to wheat.  On the charts, post-report trade builds another layer of overhead resistance into the charts with selling on rallies back to $5 CZ highly likely.  Report day lows of $4.70 CZ will stand as initial support moving forward; this area was also a full two-thirds Fibonacci retracement of the July-Aug rally.  Futures are mildly oversold but not egregiously-so with an RSI in the mid 20’s.   The August gap higher was filled on the weekly chart, which may also contribute to reduced upside market enthusiasm for now.   Note, the weekly chart also features notable support around $4.65 basis any front-month contract.

","body":"\"
            The soybean market traded firmer overnight but was unable to carry that momentum into the day session despite the return of Chinese bean purchases during the biscuit break.  The buy the rumor sell the fact price action reflected the pressure from expanding harvest and strength in the dollar which is a negative influence for export sensitive commodities.  
             
            November soybeans settled 6.5 cents lower and 16 cents off the overnight high.  The chart is testing support at the lower end of its recent trading range.  The calendar spreads were firm up front as pressure from the index fund roll has abated.  The Nov-Jan spread gaining 1.5 to a 2-week high at a 14.75 carry.   In the inter-market spread action, beans lost to corn for the third session in a row following Friday’s dramatic crop report move the other direction.  Domestic bean basis was mostly steady to lower with the gut slot of harvest upon us for the next few weeks despite some short term, regional disruptions expected by rains.  The CIF bean bid at the Gulf was up 2 to +82.  
             
            Ahead of tomorrow’s NOPA crush report, the average trade estimate on September crush is 203.7 mb, down from 205.4 mb in August but up from the September of 2025 crush of 197.8 mb.  If achieved this would represent a new record for the month despite soybean supply tightness that forced some plants to reduce their crush.  Oil stocks at the end of September were estimated on average at 1.116 bln lbs down from 1.201 bln lbs in August and 1.243 bln lbs in September of 2025.  If realized, this would be the tightest monthly oil stocks since November of 2024. 
             
            Tomorrow, we’ll also get a monthly Conab update on Brazilian production potential in the morning.   It is too early in the growing\\\/planting season down there to make any meaningful adjustments to crop expectations.  Planting is off to a positive start is about all you can say. 
             
            In the product trade, bean oil has been under pressure since yesterday’s midday EPA announcement including a .96 drop today.  The EPA announced a 100% reallocation of the 2025 SREs with the only question being whether those volumes are divided between 2026 and 2027 or they all fall into the 2027 compliance year.  Despite the negative price response in bean oil, this is seen as a positive demand outcome by restoring 100% of the biofuel volume impacted by the SREs.  The oil share spread retreated to a 2.5 week low to 47.91%.  Meal was the beneficiary of the oil share spreading which supported a $1.3 flat price gain and a bounce back in the bull spreads.  Board crush margins were a penny easier to $2.62\\\/bushel. 
             
            Elsewhere in the news, the USDA reported an 8 am flash sale of 470 tmt of beans to China. <\\\/span>

            The crop progress report showed soybean conditions were unchanged at 47% G\\\/E with P\\\/VP steady at 14%.   92% of the crop is dropping leaves vs the five-year avg of 94%. Bean harvest moved up 21% to 46% complete but remains behind the five-year avg of 50%.  The delays compared to the 5 year averages are most pronounced in IA (-28%), KS (-10%), MI (-11%), NE (-29%), OH (-10%), and SD (-12%).
             
            Brazil soybean exports in October are projected to reach 6.55 mmt vs. 6.18 mmt estimated the previous week, according to Anec.  Meal exports 2.55 mmt vs. 2.09 mmt.  Corn exports 6.41 mmt vs. 5.34 mmt.
             
            “ASA applauds Administrator Zeldin and the Trump Administration for keeping their commitment to farmers and proposing to restore 100% of biofuel volume impacted by 2025 small refinery exemption actions,” said ASA Vice President Dave Walton, an Iowa soybean farmer. “Soybean farmers are navigating a tough farm economy, and the administration’s strong domestic biofuel policies will continue to drive much-needed market demand in the U.S. We are encouraged by today’s proposal and urge EPA to get it across the finish line quickly.”  ASA urges EPA to finalize this supplemental rulemaking to reallocate biofuel volumes as quickly as possible.

            Futures:<\\\/span><\\\/u><\\\/em><\\\/strong><\\\/p>

            Outside market influence seemed prevalent during the early part of the day as the US Dollar rallied into a fresh 18-month high following the CPI data that showed inflation was hotter than expected with traders now pricing an almost 50% chance for an Oct rate hike. But the wheat markets battled back over the latter half of the day and finished well off their lows and right up near their highs for the day.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            Dec Chicago wheat traded four lower early in the night and slipped to six lower during the early morning before rallying to within a penny of even late, only to weaken into the pause and finish four lower. Price action through the early part of the day stayed between unchanged and six lower. A mid-morning eight-cent pop sparked a rally that continued into the final hour, with the market making their session’s highs near the close before finishing four higher. <\\\/span>Dec KC wheat traded four lower early in the night and slipped to seven lower during the early morning before rallying a nickel, only to weaken again into the pause and finish five lower. After a mostly three to seven lower start to the day, futures fell to nine lower, and in doing so, moved into a three-month low. But then the market found a bid late morning and futures rallied more than ten cents, extending gains to four cents into the close before finishing three higher. <\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            Headline news:<\\\/span><\\\/u><\\\/em><\\\/strong><\\\/p>

            USDA weekly export sales will be out Friday morning, delayed one day because of Monday’s gov’t Holiday.  <\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            France Agrimer raised their forecast for French soft wheat exports outside the EU by 200 TMT up to 6.5 MMT and lowered their forecast for exports inside the EU by 100 TMT down to 7.0 MMT. They also lowered their 2026\\\/27 soft wheat ending stocks forecast by 300 TMT down to 2.7 MMT.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            Ukraine’s winter wheat planting is said to be more than 67% complete as of Tuesday, with more than 3 mil hectares planted.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/span><\\\/u><\\\/em><\\\/strong><\\\/p>

            Export business around this week:<\\\/span><\\\/u><\\\/em><\\\/strong> <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            ** Algeria’s OAIC is now thought to have bought upwards of 720 TMT of opt origin milling wheat in their tender that closed on Tuesday. Sources include Baltic Sea region wheat, including Russian supplies shipped from Baltic ports, plus Romanian, Bulgarian and Argentine wheat. Purchases were thought to be between $326 and $326.50\\\/mt C&F. In their last reported milling wheat import tender in mid-Sept, the OAIC bought ~ 500 TMT, paying between $319 and $321\\\/mt C&F. Meaning they paid a higher price in this tender than they paid a month ago, despite futures falling around 70 cents.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

             <\\\/span><\\\/p>

            ** Jordan passed on all offers and did not make a purchase in their 120 TMT opt origin milling wheat tender.<\\\/span><\\\/p>

            Business activity rose sharply in New York State in October, according to firms responding to the <\\\/span>Empire State Manufacturing Survey<\\\/em>. The headline general business conditions index climbed eighteen points to 25.5, its highest level in nearly five years. 

            New orders increased markedly and shipments grew. Unfilled orders rose, delivery times lengthened substantially, and supply availability worsened further. Inventories increased. Employment continued to rise modestly and the average workweek rose. The pace of input and selling price increases remained elevated.
